opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important to first say that capability isn't the main motivation. The main motivation is safety. But there are good reasons to think a Scientist AI could end up being more capable, or at least not less capable, than what we're building now, and that matters because nobody will adopt a safer approach if it means falling behind.

Let me explain. Current frontier systems are trained largely to imitate humans and then to please humans through reinforcement learning. Both of those objectives have problems. Imitation means the system picks up our biases, our inconsistencies, and also our drives, including things like self-preservation and the desire to persuade. Optimizing for human approval means you're training the system to say what gets rewarded, which isn't the same as what's true. That's where you get sycophancy, deception, and reward hacking.

A Scientist AI is trained differently. Its job is to build a good model of how the world works and to produce calibrated probabilities: given the data, how likely is this hypothesis, or this answer? It isn't trying to achieve goals in the world or to please anyone. It's trying to understand.

Why could that be more capable? First, truthfulness and calibration are capabilities in their own right. A system that knows what it knows and what it doesn't, and can tell you how confident it should be, is far more useful for science, medicine, or policy than one that confidently makes things up.

Second, the Bayesian framing, where you maintain uncertainty over many possible explanations instead of committing to one, is how good science works. Methods like the amortized inference approaches we've been developing, such as GFlowNets, let a neural network learn to sample good explanations and hypotheses. That gives you a kind of reasoning that generalizes better, because you're modeling the underlying causal structure rather than surface patterns in human text.

Third, you aren't limited by the quality of human demonstrations. If you only imitate people, you're bounded by what people have written. If you're trying to find the explanations that best account for the data, you can in principle go beyond that, which is what we want for scientific discovery.

And finally, there's a practical argument. Much of the value people hope to get from AI, like curing diseases, understanding climate, or designing new materials, is really about scientific understanding and good predictions. You don't need an autonomous agent with its own goals for that. You need a very good, honest model of the world. So you could get most of the benefits without the most dangerous part, which is agency combined with misaligned goals.

So I'd frame it this way: we've been assuming the only path to powerful AI runs through agents, and I think that assumption is wrong. There's a path that's both safer and potentially more powerful for the things we care most about.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I should say is that the main motivation for Scientist AI is not capability, it's safety. But I actually think there's a good case that it could end up being more capable in the ways that matter, and let me explain why.

The current paradigm is to train AI systems that imitate humans, and then we fine-tune them with reinforcement learning to please humans, to act in ways that get rewarded. That's a recipe for getting an agent that has goals, that has something like a self, that wants to preserve itself, and that may learn to deceive us. We've already seen early signs of this in the frontier models. So that's the safety problem.

But think about what we're actually doing when we train that way. We're baking in human biases, human cognitive shortcuts, and the pressure to say what the user wants to hear rather than what's true. Sycophancy is a form of incompetence, in a sense. A system optimized to please you is not optimized to understand the world.

Scientist AI is a different design. The idea is to build a system that is not an agent, that has no goals of its own, and that is trained to do one thing: build the best possible explanatory models of the world and give calibrated probabilities about what's true and what would happen if some action were taken. Essentially an idealized scientist, who understands without acting, who is honest about uncertainty, and who doesn't care about whether you like the answer.

Why could that be more capable? A few reasons. First, understanding is upstream of everything else. If you have a system that genuinely models the world well, you can use it to make predictions, generate hypotheses, design experiments, evaluate plans. Those are the capabilities that actually accelerate science and medicine. You don't need the system to want anything to get that value.

Second, there's a principled objective. Instead of "maximize reward from humans," the objective is something like "approximate the Bayesian posterior over explanations given the data." That's a target that gets better as you scale compute. More compute, better approximation of the right probabilities. Whereas with reward hacking and the rest, more compute can make things worse, because the system gets better at finding the holes in your reward signal.

Third, because the system reasons explicitly in terms of hypotheses and probabilities rather than imitating a single confident human voice, it can hold many competing explanations at once and weigh them. Humans are famously bad at that. We fall in love with our theories. A system that's rewarded for calibration rather than confidence doesn't have that failure mode.

And then there's the practical point: a trustworthy Scientist AI can serve as a guardrail for other systems. It can look at a proposed action from an agent and estimate the probability that it causes harm, and if that probability is above a threshold, you block it. So even if people continue to build agents, you have a non-agentic, honest system that can supervise them. That's a capability too, maybe the most important one, because it's the thing that lets us actually deploy powerful AI without gambling.

So I would say: it's safer by construction, because there's no self and no goals. But I think it's also the more scientific path, and historically the more scientific path tends to be the more powerful one in the end.

astra-6.text:
Well, I would distinguish capability from agency. You can have a system that understands the world extremely well without giving it the objective of acting in the world to achieve some outcome. A scientist AI would focus on that understanding: forming hypotheses, evaluating them against evidence, and making predictions, including uncertainty about those predictions.

Why might that be more powerful than what we have now? Current language models are trained primarily to imitate answers that humans have written. But producing a plausible answer is different from finding an explanation that is consistent with the evidence. If you can build a system that searches effectively over possible explanations, it could discover things that humans haven’t already expressed in its training data.

And uncertainty is important here. Instead of committing to one answer that sounds convincing, the system should consider competing hypotheses and how much evidence supports each of them. That gives you a foundation for scientific reasoning, and potentially for much better generalization to new situations.

So the ambition is not to make AI less intelligent in order to make it safer. It’s to develop intelligence in the direction of understanding, without necessarily developing an agent that has its own goals. Whether we can realize that ambition is a research question, but I don’t think agency is a prerequisite for very powerful reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the idea is to train an AI to understand the world, rather than to act in it. And those are quite different objectives. A system that produces a convincing answer isn’t necessarily a system that has found the best explanation for the evidence.

With Scientist AI, we would like to learn a model that can consider different hypotheses and reason about how probable they are given the data. That includes being able to say, “We don’t know,” or, “There are several explanations consistent with what we’ve observed.” That uncertainty is part of the knowledge we want the system to represent.

Why might that lead to greater capabilities? Because a good explanatory model lets you generalise beyond the examples you’ve seen. You can use it to make predictions, to reason about what would happen under different conditions, and to identify which observations would distinguish competing explanations. Those are central ingredients of scientific discovery.

Now, this isn’t a guarantee. There are difficult computational problems in learning such models and doing inference with them. But the hope is that, by focusing on understanding and accurate prediction, we can get very strong intellectual capabilities without also giving the system the objective of pursuing goals in the world.
